stories.title: Get Ready for a Super Hot El Nino!
stories.headline_kid: Scientists say there's a 98% chance of a super-strong El Nino hitting our region soon, bringing extra heat, drier weather, and higher prices.
summary: El Nino is a natural weather pattern that happens every few years when parts of the ocean get warmer than usual. When it happens, Southeast Asia often becomes hotter and drier than normal — like someone turning up the oven dial for the whole region.

Weather experts now say there is a 98 per cent chance — almost certain — that a 'very strong' El Nino will hit between October and December this year. The last time this happened, in 2015-2016, it caused terrible wildfires and thick haze across the region.

This matters because hot, dry weather can dry up farms, spark more forest fires (some are already burning in Indonesia), and push up the price of food like rice and vegetables. It could also mean more haze days for Singapore, just like we've seen recently.

Singapore's agencies are watching the situation closely and preparing plans for water supply, health advisories, and haze management. Families may need to budget a little more for groceries and electricity bills as everyone uses more air-con to stay cool.

lenses.friends: Outdoor school activities like sports day or excursions might be adjusted if the heat or haze gets bad.
lenses.nation: Singapore's government agencies are preparing measures for water supply, public health, and haze control ahead of time.
lenses.world: Countries across Southeast Asia may face wildfires, water shortages, and rising food costs because of the extreme heat.

stories.title: Will AirAsia's Money Troubles Affect Your Next Holiday Flight?
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia's government is quietly checking if budget airline AirAsia has money troubles, and asking other airlines if they could take over its flights.
summary: AirAsia is a popular budget airline that many Singaporean families use for cheap flights to places like Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. Lately, there have been concerns about the airline's financial health.

According to sources, the Malaysian government has asked two rival airlines — Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air — whether they could take over some of AirAsia's routes and passengers if needed. This is like a teacher quietly checking if a classmate needs extra help before a problem gets worse.

This doesn't mean AirAsia is closing down right away. It simply shows that officials are being careful and planning ahead in case things change. If other airlines do step in, flight schedules or ticket prices on some routes could shift.
For Singapore families who love budget travel, this is a story worth keeping an eye on, especially if you have upcoming trips booked with AirAsia.

lenses.family: Parents planning budget holidays may want to double-check bookings and watch for updates.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose families are flying soon might be talking about this at school.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies on good flight connections with our neighbours, so changes in Malaysia's airline industry can affect travel options from Changi Airport too.
lenses.world: This shows how competition and money problems can affect budget airlines that many people across Asia depend on.

stories.title: Malaysia's Politics Get Tense — Why Singapore Is Watching
stories.headline_kid: A top Malaysian political leader wants an early election, putting pressure on the Prime Minister — and it matters to Singapore because Malaysia is our closest neighbour.
summary: In Malaysia, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim leads the government. But UMNO party chief Zahid Hamidi believes political momentum is now on his side and is pushing hard for an early general election.

A commentator explains that Anwar can buy some time by resisting this pressure, but he will still need a real plan to keep his coalition partners happy — a bit like a class monitor needing to keep classmates on his side before an election for prefects.

Why should Singapore kids care? Malaysia is our nearest neighbour, connected by the Causeway that thousands of people cross every day for work and school. Political changes there can affect trade, business deals, and even how smoothly the Causeway runs.

If a sudden election happens, there could be short-term disruptions while politics plays out. But for most Singaporean families, daily life is expected to continue as normal — it's just something worth understanding, since what happens next door often affects us too.

lenses.family: Parents may discuss how this affects business, trade, or relatives who cross the Causeway for work.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents work across the border might notice changes if there's political uncertainty.
lenses.nation: Singapore's economy is closely linked to Malaysia through trade, the Causeway, and shared resources.
lenses.world: This shows how elections and political competition work in a democracy, and how they can ripple beyond one country's borders.

stories.title: New US Rules Could Make Oil More Expensive Worldwide
stories.headline_kid: America's lawmakers just passed a tough new law that could raise oil prices around the world — and that could affect petrol prices here in Singapore too.
summary: The US Congress, which is like America's Parliament, has passed a new law giving President Trump the power to charge extra taxes — called tariffs — of up to 100 per cent on countries that buy a lot of oil and gas from Russia. This is meant to pressure Russia over its ongoing war in Ukraine.

Big countries like China and India buy huge amounts of Russian oil. If they get hit with these tariffs, buying and selling oil could become more complicated and expensive worldwide — similar to how an extra toll makes a shortcut road more costly to use.

Singapore doesn't have its own oil wells, so we import fuel from other countries. If global oil prices rise because of this new law, petrol at the pump, bus and taxi fares, and even the cost of shipping goods could all creep up.

This law hasn't actually been used yet — it's now up to President Trump to decide when and how to apply it. Economists around the world, including in Singapore, will be watching closely to see what happens next.

lenses.nation: Singapore, which imports all its oil, closely watches global energy prices since they affect the whole economy.
lenses.world: This shows how political decisions between powerful countries can ripple into daily costs for people everywhere.

stories.title: Meet the Secret Team Behind Singapore's Famous Night Race
stories.headline_kid: The Singapore Grand Prix isn't just three exciting nights of racing — a whole team works all year round to make it happen safely.
summary: The Singapore Grand Prix is a famous Formula 1 night race held at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, watched by millions of people around the world. Many of us have seen its bright lights and fireworks lighting up the sky.

But behind the glamorous three-day race weekend, a dedicated team works all year long. Their jobs include handling ticket sales, planning for crowd safety among huge numbers of spectators, managing event operations, and even keeping an eye on world news in case anything — like weather or security concerns — could affect the race.

This shows just how much careful planning and teamwork goes into hosting a major global sporting event. It's a bit like organising a giant school sports day, but multiplied thousands of times in size and complexity.

Hosting the F1 race successfully year after year is something Singapore is proud of. It shows off our nation's ability to run world-class events smoothly, boosts tourism, and gives local event professionals a chance to shine on the world stage.
